claims.text: A coupled DFT and machine-learning framework can predict the electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr within ±5% of experiment.
The proposed accuracy applies across both 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The framework explicitly accounts for point defects and 1 wt.% oxygen.
The modeled samples contain realistic distributions of point defects.
The oxygen-containing samples have homogeneous incorporation of 1 wt.% oxygen.
Machine-learning corrections will be calibrated using conductivity data with characterized defect concentrations, clustering, and oxygen effects.
The 0–200 K regime is governed in part by low-temperature quantum and defect scattering effects.
The 300–1200 K regime is governed in part by phonon and impurity scattering.
Local lattice distortions, point-defect states, and oxygen-induced impurity states modulate electronic energy levels and carrier-scattering rates.
Standard DFT supplies the base electronic structure of defect-free HfNbTaTiZr.
An experimentally calibrated ML model can correct energy-level shifts and scattering probabilities caused by defects, disorder, and oxygen clustering.
Including real microstructural imperfections overcomes limitations of analytical approaches that assume ideal lattices.
The conductivity at 400 K is expected to be approximately 350 S/m.
The sample containing 1 wt.% oxygen will exhibit additional carrier scattering relative to a defect-free sample.
Existing ideal-crystal analytical predictions deviate significantly from measured conductivity because they neglect scattering from realistic defects and oxygen impurities.
Predictions above 1200 K are extrapolative and may not retain the claimed accuracy.
Variability in defect distributions and oxygen clustering may change the calibration and resulting error margin.
A prediction error greater than ±5% at 400 K would falsify the accuracy hypothesis.
A deviation greater than 20 S/m from 350 S/m is treated as equivalent to an error greater than ±5%.

contradictions.description: At a 350 S/m benchmark, ±5% is ±17.5 S/m, not ±20 S/m. Thus the stated percentage criterion and the numerical falsification criterion are inconsistent.

The ML component is trained on experimental conductivity data, but the 400 K benchmark is not explicitly held out from training. The proposed falsification measurement could therefore overlap with calibration data rather than constitute the requested held-out test.
